title: Washington Is Quietly Closing Every Door That Indian Professionals Use to Stay in America
excerpt: A $100,000 H-1B fee, the end of 'Duration of Status' for students, green card applicants told to go home first, and proposed bills to kill the H-1B-to-green-card pipeline — it's not one policy change, it's a systematic overhaul.
body:
No single headline captured it. But over the past eight weeks, Washington has moved on at least four separate fronts to tighten, restrict, or fundamentally reshape the immigration pathways that hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals depend on to live and work in the United States.

Taken individually, each measure drew some coverage and a round of anxious WhatsApp forwards in Indian-American group chats. Taken together, they represent the most aggressive restructuring of skilled immigration in a generation — and the overwhelming majority of people affected are Indian.

## The $100,000 H-1B Fee

On June 8, US District Judge Leo Sorokin ruled that the Trump administration's $100,000 filing fee on certain H-1B visa petitions was an "unauthorized tax" that exceeded the government's legal authority. For four days, employers breathed easier. Then, on June 12, Judge Sorokin issued an administrative stay of his own ruling, preserving the fee while the government appeals to the First Circuit.

The fee, which applies to companies where more than 15 per cent of workers are H-1B or L-1 visa holders, hits Indian IT services firms hardest. It effectively adds six figures to the cost of sponsoring a single worker — a sum that many mid-sized companies simply cannot absorb. The legal battle continues, and the fee remains in force.

## Duration of Status: Gone

On May 5, the Department of Homeland Security proposed eliminating "Duration of Status" — the decades-old framework that lets international students stay in the US as long as they maintain their F-1 visa status and comply with requirements. Under the proposed rule, most students would receive a fixed admission period of up to four years. Any extension — to finish a programme, to do OPT, to pursue STEM OPT — would require filing a formal application with USCIS.



> **"Thousands who fail the H-1B lottery currently enrol in "Day 1 CPT" programmes — a second master's degree that allows them to keep working legally while they try again."**


The proposed rule also cuts the post-programme grace period from 60 days to 30 days and bars graduate students from switching programmes. The rule cleared its final pre-publication review on June 17 and is expected to take effect by September 2026 — just in time for fall arrivals.

For Indians, who are the largest or second-largest international student group in the US, the change closes a critical safety valve. Thousands who fail the H-1B lottery currently enrol in "Day 1 CPT" programmes — a second master's degree that allows them to keep working legally while they try again. Under the new rules, anyone who already holds a master's degree would be ineligible to pursue another at the same level.

"For anyone who already has a master's degree, they are not going to be able to go back and say, 'I need another master's degree because I need work authorisation to continue working,'" said Danielle Goldman, CEO of immigration firm Build.

## Green Card? Go Home First.

On May 22, USCIS announced that "adjustment of status" — the process by which someone already in the US on a temporary visa transitions to permanent residency without leaving — will now be treated as "an extraordinary form of relief" granted only in limited cases. The default expectation is that green card applicants must return to their home country and process their applications through a US consulate abroad.

For the estimated one million-plus Indians in the employment-based green card backlog, many of whom have lived and worked in the US for a decade or more, this is seismic. Leaving the country means uprooting children from schools, vacating jobs, and re-entering a queue that — for Indian-born EB-2 applicants — currently stretches back to September 2013. The risk of something going wrong at a consulate interview, after years of building a life in America, is not theoretical.

## The Legislative Push

In Congress, at least a dozen Republican lawmakers have backed four separate bills this year targeting the H-1B programme. The most aggressive, introduced by Representative Chip Roy of Texas on June 4, would cut the maximum H-1B stay from six years to two, end the H-1B-to-green-card pathway entirely, eliminate the Optional Practical Training programme, and cap admissions from any single country at seven per cent of the annual allocation.

Representative Eli Crane of Arizona has proposed a three-year pause on H-1B issuances altogether.

None of these bills has passed, and most face long odds. But their proliferation signals a political environment in which restricting skilled immigration is no longer a fringe position — it is a competitive platform within the Republican caucus.

## The Pattern

Each of these moves targets a different stage of the same pipeline: student visas at entry, work visas at employment, and green cards at settlement. The net effect is to narrow every pathway that Indian professionals have used, in sequence, to build careers and families in the United States.

US Ambassador Sergio Gor has insisted the H-1B review is "not directed at any particular country." But the numbers tell a different story. Indians received roughly 72 per cent of H-1B visas in the most recent fiscal year. Indians make up the largest share of the employment-based green card backlog. Indian students are the most likely to use OPT and STEM OPT.

When every door narrows, the people who use every door the most feel it first. For the Indian diaspora in America, the walls are closing in — and no single headline is big enough to say so.
